summary: A short, static label on a thing — a status, a count, a category.

pairs.dont: Make a badge clickable, or use one as a filter chip.
pairs.do: Use Chip for something selectable and Button for something that acts.
pairs.why: A badge is a label on a thing, not a thing to press. Making one clickable gives it no focus ring, no hit area and no keyboard route.

pairs.dont: Signal status with colour and nothing else.
pairs.do: Keep the word — "Healthy", "Critical" — and add the dot if it helps.
pairs.why: Colour alone fails for anyone who cannot separate the hues, and a badge is small enough that the hue is all there is. The word is the signal; the colour reinforces it.

pairs.dont: Put three badges in a row on the same object.
pairs.do: Show the one that changes what the reader does next.
pairs.why: Badges are loud by design. Three of them compete, and the reader ends up scanning past all three.

pairs.dont: Write a sentence in a badge.
pairs.do: One or two words. Put the detail in the text beside it.
pairs.why: A badge does not wrap gracefully and cannot be read at a glance once it is longer than its container is wide.

pairs.dont: Use emphasis badges everywhere because they read more clearly.
pairs.do: Keep emphasis for the exception, and subtle for the rest.
pairs.why: The solid fill is the loudest thing on most surfaces. Used for every row it becomes the background, and the one that matters disappears into it.

pairs.dont: Reach for outline expecting a quieter red or green.
pairs.do: Use subtle for a quiet coloured badge; outline is deliberately neutral.
pairs.why: Outline renders identically for all five colours — neutral fill, neutral border, neutral text. Choosing it discards the colour rather than muting it.

a11y: The dot is aria-hidden. A badge's meaning is its text — colour and dot are reinforcement, never the signal.
Badge is not a live region. A count that changes while the page is open announces nothing unless the surrounding component says so.
